pages.name: The heater test
pages.text: Two identical 10 Ω heaters: the left on AC that peaks at 100 V, the right on a steady DC level. The power in each is the voltage squared ÷ 10, moment by moment, so the AC power comes in humps, on the backward half too, because a minus squared is a plus. Its heat is the humps' average, the dashed line. Drag the DC level and watch the heat bars.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 500 W. The DC one sits at 50 V, giving 250 W.

pages.name: Where they match
pages.task: At what DC level do the two heat bars match?
pages.why: The AC heater averages half its 1000 W top, 500 W. A steady level gives 500 W when its square is 500 × 10 = 5000, and that is near 70.7 V. A steady 100 V gives 1000 W all the time, while the wave touches 100 V only for an instant. The 63.7 V is the wave's plain average over half a cycle, a hump's area over its width, 2 ÷ π of the peak (Calculus fundamentals' mid-ordinate rule). It gives only about 406 W, because heat goes with the square.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 500 W. The DC one sits at 70.7 V, giving 500 W, the same heat.

pages.name: Why 70.7 V
pages.text: At 70.7 V the DC heater's flat power lies along the AC humps' dashed average, 500 W, and the bars match. That is Calculus fundamentals' recipe, worked under the graph: square the wave, take the mean, take the root. This steady equivalent is the [[rms value]], root mean square. For a sine it is about 0.707 of the peak, 1 ÷ √2.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 500 W. The DC one sits at 70.7 V, giving 500 W, the same heat.

pages.name: Peak against steady
pages.task: The DC level is now 100 V, the AC wave's peak. How does the DC heater's heat compare with the AC heater's?
pages.why: A steady 100 V gives 100² ÷ 10 = 1000 W the whole time. The AC heater reaches 1000 W only at the top of each wave and averages half of it, 500 W. So the DC gives twice the heat. 1.41 is the ratio of the voltages, and heat goes with its square, about 2.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 500 W. The DC one sits at 100 V, giving 1000 W.

pages.name: Other shapes
pages.text: The 0.707 belongs to the sine. A square wave sits at its full 100 V all but the instant it flips, so its power is a flat 1000 W and the bars match at 100 V, a ratio of 1.0. A triangle spends more time low down: the mean of a ramp's square is a third of its top's (Calculus fundamentals). Switch the shape and watch the match move.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a square wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 1000 W. The DC one sits at 100 V, giving 1000 W, the same heat.

pages.name: The triangle
pages.task: The AC heater now runs on a triangle wave with an 80 V peak. What steady DC heats its twin just as much?
pages.why: The triangle's power humps top out at 80² ÷ 10 = 640 W and average a third of that, 213 W. A steady level gives 213 W at 80 ÷ √3, near 46.2 V, the triangle's 0.577 of the peak. 56.6 V uses the sine's 0.707 on the wrong shape, and 40 V is the triangle's plain average over half a cycle, which forgets the square.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a triangle wave peaking at 80 V. Its average heat is 213 W. The DC one sits at 46.2 V, giving 213 W, the same heat.

pages.name: Mains
pages.text: Now the mains card: 230 V mains on a 1 kW heater of 230² ÷ 1000 = 52.9 Ω. A steady 230 V of DC gives its twin the same 1000 W, so the 230 V on the label is the rms value. The wave itself climbs above the DC line. How far?
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 52.9 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 325 V. Its average heat is 1000 W. The DC one sits at 230 V, giving 1000 W, the same heat.

pages.name: The top of the wave
pages.task: This heater runs on 230 V mains, and 230 V of DC heats its twin just as much. How high does the mains wave climb at the top of each cycle?
pages.why: 230 V is the rms value, the steady DC that gives the same heat. For a sine the peak is √2 times bigger, 230 × 1.41, about 325 V. Dividing by √2 instead gives 163 V, the wrong way round. So everything on the supply, insulation included, meets 325 V at the top of every cycle and −325 V at the bottom, a swing of 650 V. A ship's 440 V system, for example, peaks at 440 × √2 = 622 V.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 52.9 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 325 V. Its average heat is 1000 W. The DC one sits at 230 V, giving 1000 W, the same heat.

pages.name: The meter
pages.text: Many analogue meters do not square the wave. The needle follows its average folded all one way, 0.637 (2 ÷ π) of the peak on a sine, and the scale is marked up by the sine's [[form factor]], rms ÷ average, 0.707 ÷ 0.637 = 1.11. So on a sine it reads 230 V. Now watch a triangle with the same 325 V peak, and try the square.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 52.9 ohms. The AC one runs on a triangle wave peaking at 325 V. Its average heat is 666 W. The DC one sits at 188 V, giving 666 W, the same heat. An average-reading meter reads 180 V.

pages.name: A meter on a square
pages.task: An average-reading meter shows 111 V on this square wave, which peaks at 100 V. What is its rms value?
pages.why: A square wave sits at its full 100 V all the time, one way or the other, so it heats like a steady 100 V. Its rms value is its peak, 100 V. The meter's 1.11 mark-up is meant for a sine, so on a square it over-reads, 111 V. 70.7 V would use the sine's ratio on the wrong shape.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 10 ohms. The AC one runs on a square wave peaking at 100 V. Its average heat is 1000 W. The DC one sits at 100 V, giving 1000 W, the same heat. An average-reading meter reads 111 V.

pages.name: 230 V of DC
pages.task: Mixed. A 1 kW heater rated at 230 V is run from a 230 V DC supply instead of mains. What does it give?
pages.why: The 230 V of mains is an rms figure, the steady DC that heats a resistance just as much. So 230 V of DC gives the same 1 kW. The 2 kW is the mains heater's power for an instant at the top of each wave, not its average.
pages.alt: Two identical heaters of 52.9 ohms. The AC one runs on a sine wave peaking at 325 V. Its average heat is 1000 W. The DC one sits at 230 V, giving 1000 W, the same heat.

pages.name: Two meters
pages.task: Mixed. On one supply, with both meters in calibration, an average-reading meter shows 167 V and a true-rms meter shows 173 V. What is going on?
pages.answer: It is not a sine, and 173 V sets the heat
pages.why: Both meters are fine. The average-reading meter's 1.11 mark-up is right only on a sine, so the two disagree when the wave is another shape. Here it is a triangle with a 300 V peak. The true-rms meter works out the heating value, so 173 V is the figure that sets the heat.
